{{Short description|Nuclear physicist (1924–1989)}}
{{Use American English|date=August 2026}}
[[File:Hoffman-frederic de.jpg|thumb|Frederic de Hoffman Los Alamos badge]]
'''Frederic de Hoffmann''' (July 8, 1924 – October 4, 1989) was an Austrian-born American [[nuclear physicist]] who worked on the [[Manhattan Project]]. He was born in [[Vienna]], [[Austria]] and died in [[San Diego]], [[California]].<ref name="Obituary">{{cite news
| last = Stevens
| first = William K.
| title = Frederic de Hoffmann, 65, Dies; Physicist and Salk Institute Chief
| place =
| pages =
| language =
| work = [[New York Times]]
| date = 1989-10-07
| url = https://www.nytimes.com/1989/10/07/obituaries/frederic-de-hoffmann-65-dies-physicist-and-salk-institute-chief.html
| accessdate = 2009-07-09}}</ref> He came to the [[United States of America]] in 1941 and graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1945. He also received a master's in 1947 and a doctorate in 1948.<ref name="Obituary"/> Before graduating, de Hoffmann was sent to [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] in 1944 where he assisted [[Edward Teller]] in the development of the [[Hydrogen bomb]].<ref name="Obituary"/> Frederic de Hoffmann was an advocate of peaceful atomic energy.<ref name="Obituary"/>

After leaving Los Alamos, de Hoffmann collaborated with [[Hans Bethe]] and [[Silvan Schweber]] on a textbook called ''Mesons and Fields'' and became chairman of the Committee of Senior Reviewers of the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission]].<ref name="GDyson31">{{Cite book
  | last = Dyson
  | first = George
  | authorlink = George Dyson (science historian)
  | title = Project Orion
  | publisher = Penguin Books
  | date = 2002
  | location = Great Britain
  | pages = 31}}</ref> He received his PhD from [[Julian Schwinger]] in 1948.<ref name="MehraMilton">{{Cite book
  | last = Mehra
  | first = Jagdish
  |last2=Milton |first2= Kimball A.
  | title = Climbing the Mountain: The Scientific Biography of Julian Schwinger
  | publisher = Oxford University Press
  | date = 2000
  | pages = 153
  | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=M_ONmDLmGO4C&dq=%22frederic+de+hoffmann%22&pg=PA153
  | isbn = 0-19-850658-9}}</ref>

Frederic De Hoffmann moved to the [[General Dynamics Corporation]] in 1955.<ref name="Obituary"/> That year he was recruited by [[John Jay Hopkins]] to found [[General Atomics]] and serve as its first president.<ref name="Obituary"/><ref name="Seidel">{{Cite journal
  | last = Seidel
  | first = Robert W.
  | title = Technology transfer: Half-way houses
  | issue = 17
  | publisher = Department of Energy
  | date = May 1995
  | doi = 10.2172/105070 |osti=105070
 | url = http://www.osti.gov/bridge/purl.cover.jsp;jsessionid=C17C7D666E7DADF5A024E6C3D6FF7022?purl=/105070-eHzsZs/webviewable/
  | accessdate = 2010-03-12}}</ref> This organization's purpose was to manufacture nuclear reactors for energy production, and sell them on the open market.<ref name="Ob2">{{Cite news
  | title = Frederic de Hoffmann
  | newspaper = Sarasota herald-Tribune
  | pages = 7B
  | date = 1989-10-07
  | url = https://news.google.com.au/newspapers?id=gbYcAAAAIBAJ&sjid=VHoEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6267,1698262&dq=frederic-de-hoffmann&hl=en
  | accessdate = 2010-03-12}}</ref> In the late '50s he organized [[Project Orion (nuclear propulsion)|Project Orion]], a plan for a spaceship to be propelled by nuclear bombs.<ref name="FDyson">{{Cite book
  | last = Dyson
  | first = Freeman J.
  | authorlink = Freeman Dyson
  | title = Selected papers of Freeman Dyson with commentary
  | publisher = American Mathematical Society
  | date = 1996
  | location = United States
  | pages = 26
  | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=nnyNUidX1OMC&dq=%22frederic+de+hoffmann%22+orion&pg=PA26
| isbn = 9780821805619
 }}</ref>

He helped found the [[University of California]]'s campus in [[San Diego]], the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref name="Seidel"/>

De Hoffmann joined the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] in 1970 and served as its president for 18 years.<ref name="Obituary"/> He was also the chairman and chief executive officer of the Salk Institute Biotechnology-Industry Associates Inc.<ref name="Ob2"/> When de Hoffmann retired in 1988 he was named the institute's president emeritus.<ref name="Ob2"/> He died in 1989 of [[AIDS]],<ref name="Obituary"/> which he contracted in 1984 from an infected [[blood transfusion]] he received during surgery.<ref name="Ob3">{{Cite news
  | title = Many fall victim to AIDS
  | newspaper = Gadsden Times
  | pages = A18
  | date = 1989-12-31
  | url = https://news.google.com.au/newspapers?id=vWgfAAAAIBAJ&sjid=7dQEAAAAIBAJ&pg=2823,4152402&dq=frederic-de-hoffmann&hl=en
  | accessdate = 2010-03-12}}</ref>
